name: Growth and Reinvestment Consistency

positioning.oneLineSummary: Makes growth pay for the operating assets, working capital, R&D, acquisition, and capacity needed to produce it.
positioning.productLabel: Growth and Reinvestment Consistency Lens — based on Aswath Damodaran's public valuation materials
notAClaimOf: sales-to-capital being universal across business models
accounting expense treatment measuring economic reinvestment correctly

attribution.display: Based on Aswath Damodaran's public valuation materials

neutralParaphrase: Revenue and margin growth require reinvestment. A young-company model can use a sales-to-capital relationship to connect incremental revenue to capital needs, but the economic definition of capital must reflect the business model, including working capital, capacity, capitalized R&D, customer acquisition, and other assets that accounting may expense.

locator.value: PDF pp. 24-30: revenue and margin forecasts, reinvestment, and sales-to-capital implementation
PDF pp. 30-39: stable reinvestment, return on capital, terminal value, and sensitivity

requiredConditions: Revenue growth and reinvestment use the same periods, currency, and scope.
Economic investment is distinguished from accounting expense classification.
Working capital, capacity, R&D, customer acquisition, and acquisition spend are considered where material.
Stable growth and return on capital imply a consistent stable reinvestment rate.

requiredEvidence.description: Historical or current relationship between incremental revenue and operating investment.
Identification of the assets and expenses that economically create future revenue for this business model.
Scenario-specific reinvestment schedule connected to revenue and margin forecasts.
Stable-state return on capital and reinvestment assumptions benchmarked to competition and durability.

decisionQuestions: What investments create the projected revenue in this business?
What sales-to-capital or equivalent driver is implied each year?
Are R&D, software, brand, customer acquisition, inventory, or capacity economically capitalized where appropriate?
Does margin improvement remove costs that are still needed for growth?
Is the funding plan sufficient for the modeled reinvestment and runway?
Are stable growth, reinvestment, and return on capital mathematically consistent?
positiveSignals: Historical or cohort evidence connects incremental spend to incremental revenue.
The model recognizes intangible and working-capital investment.
Scenario-specific capital needs reconcile to runway and financing.
Growth slows or investment rises when capacity becomes constrained.
Stable reinvestment follows from a defensible stable return on capital.
redFlags: Revenue grows rapidly while capital needs approach zero without evidence.
All R&D or customer acquisition is treated as maintenance expense despite future benefits.
Hardware, inventory, implementation, or working capital is absent from growth economics.
Margin expands only because growth investment is removed.
Terminal growth is assumed without terminal reinvestment.
disconfirmingEvidence: Past growth required materially more capital than forecast.
Customer acquisition payback or implementation burden worsens with scale.
Capacity commitments arrive earlier than the model assumes.
The company needs financing beyond the modeled plan to sustain growth.
Stable return on capital exceeds plausible competitive economics without a supported barrier.
contraindications: Do not apply one sales-to-capital ratio across unrelated business models.
Do not equate accounting capex with total economic reinvestment.
Do not double count growth investment in both cash flow and a separate discount.
Do not infer a terminal return on capital from current early-stage margins.

instructions: Map all economically relevant investment categories.
Estimate scenario-specific sales-to-capital or equivalent operating drivers.
Calculate reinvestment from incremental revenue and required assets.
Reconcile capital needs to runway and financing.
Apply stable-state consistency checks in the valuation service.

sourceReliability.low: Only a high-level budget or founder estimate is available.
sourceReliability.medium: Company financials and partial cohort or capacity evidence are available.
sourceReliability.high: Reconciled accounts, operating cohorts, capacity plans, and normalized benchmarks are verified.

evidenceStrength.medium: Major capital categories are modeled with several external priors.
evidenceStrength.high: Growth investment relationships are measured and scenario-consistent.

evidenceCoverage.medium: Capex, working capital, and major intangibles are included but stable economics are incomplete.
evidenceCoverage.high: All material investment categories, financing, and stable-state relationships are covered.

applicabilityConfidence.low: The business has no definable revenue or investment driver.
applicabilityConfidence.medium: Drivers are plausible but current data are sparse.
applicabilityConfidence.high: Revenue and economic investment units are explicit and measurable.

judgmentConfidence.low: Only a broad capital-needs warning can be stated.
judgmentConfidence.medium: The model is directionally consistent but sensitive to one material proxy.
judgmentConfidence.high: Reinvestment, growth, runway, and terminal economics reconcile under verified data.

promotionRequirements: Define and validate business-model-specific economic-capital mappings.
Backtest forecast capital needs against actual financing and operating outcomes.
empiricalQualifications: Sales-to-capital is a simplifying relationship, not a universal causal constant.
Accounting treatment can obscure intangible investment.
Financing constraints may change the attainable growth path even when project economics are attractive.

rights.notes: Formulas are standard deterministic identities described by public author materials; prose is neutral paraphrase.
